plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 1.6.1
plan.contextChunk: This figure shows the unit circle with a fixed angle c and a variable angle x measured from the positive horizontal axis, illustrating the continuity of the sine and cosine functions. Point Q(cos c, sin c) is marked in blue at angle c, and point P(cos x, sin x) is marked in red at angle x; an arrow indicates that P moves toward Q as x approaches c. A caption box at the bottom reads: As x approaches c the point P approaches the point Q. The figure provides a geometric motivation for the limits lim_{x->c} sin x = sin c and lim_{x->c} cos x = cos c, establishing that sin and cos are continuous at every point c.

interactionPlan.concept: As an angle x approaches a fixed angle c on the unit circle, the point P(cos x, sin x) approaches Q(cos c, sin c), giving the geometric reason that sine and cosine are continuous.

vertical y-axis with arrowhead pointing up
origin where the axes cross

blue point Q on the unit circle labeled Q(cos c, sin c)
red point P on the unit circle labeled P(cos x, sin x)
purple shaded sector between the rays at angles x and c
angle arc from the positive x-axis to the red radius labeled x
larger angle arc from the positive x-axis to the black radius labeled c
curved arrow near the unit circle indicating P moving toward Q

interactions.label: Angle x
interactions.teaches: Changing x moves P along the unit circle and shows that making x closer to c makes the geometric gap between P and Q shrink

interactions.label: Target angle c
interactions.teaches: Continuity of sine and cosine is not tied to one special angle: wherever Q is placed on the unit circle, nearby angles x produce nearby points P

interactions.label: Animate x approaching c from both sides
interactions.teaches: Approaching c from angles below and above c leads P to the same point Q, showing the two-sided limit behavior of sine and cosine

demo_steps.title: Start with x below c
demo_steps.narration: The blue point Q is fixed at angle c, while the red point P is at a smaller angle x. The shaded sector represents the angular difference between x and c.

demo_steps.title: Move x closer to c
demo_steps.narration: As x increases toward c, P slides along the unit circle toward Q. The shaded sector shrinks, making the distance between the coordinate pairs visually approach zero.

demo_steps.title: Change the target angle
demo_steps.narration: Now move c to a different location on the unit circle. Q, the black radius, and the label update, but the same idea remains: P approaches Q whenever x approaches c.

demo_steps.title: Watch the two-sided approach
demo_steps.narration: Run the animation to see x approach c first from one side and then from the other. In both cases, the red point P ends at the same blue point Q.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: On the unit circle, small changes in angle produce small changes in both coordinates, so cos x approaches cos c and sin x approaches sin c as x approaches c.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use a clean 2D coordinate-plane diagram with black axes and arrowheads, no grid. Draw the unit circle in bright blue with Q as a blue dot and P as a red dot. The ray to Q should be black and the ray to P red; shade the sector between them in translucent purple so it visibly shrinks as x approaches c. Place math-style labels near the points: Q(cos c, sin c) near the blue dot and P(cos x, sin x) near the red dot. Show small angle arcs at the origin labeled x and c. Keep the caption box below the diagram. During the approach animation, P should travel along the circle toward Q from both clockwise and counterclockwise directions while Q remains fixed.

authoredContext:
Recall from trigonometry that the graphs of sin x and cos x are drawn as continuous curves. We will not formally prove that these functions are continuous, but we can motivate this fact by letting c be a fixed angle in radian measure and x a variable angle in radian measure. If, as illustrated in Figure 1.6.1, the angle x approaches the angle c, then the point P(cos x,sin x) moves along the unit circle toward Q(cos c,sin c), and the coordinates of P approach the
corresponding coordinates of Q. This implies that
lim
x→c
sin x = sin c and limx→c
cos x = cos c (1)
Thus, sin x and cos x are continuous at the arbitrary point c; that is, these functions are continuous everywhere.

discrepancies: the blue unit-circle curve is drawn as a complete closed circle, whereas the source shows a partial/cropped blue circle arc with visible gaps at the left edge
the purple sector is rendered as a flat uniform translucent fill instead of the source's lighter gradient-like shading that fades toward the red radius
the curved black approach arrow near Q is shorter and differently positioned than in the source, where it is a larger arc clearly indicating P moving toward Q along the circle
the caption box and caption text are noticeably smaller and narrower relative to the main figure than in the source
the generated default view includes a prominent right-side instructional control panel/readout, which changes the static drop-in appearance compared with the source image
evaluation.notes: The main unit-circle geometry, rays, points, labels, angle arcs, and limiting concept are accurately represented, but the circle/caption proportions and sector/arrow styling are not quite faithful to the source.
action_items: Draw the blue circle as the same partial/cropped arc segments seen in the source rather than a fully closed circle.
Use a subtle purple-to-white gradient or lighter opacity variation for the sector so it resembles the source shading.
Resize and reposition the caption box/text to more closely match the large lower caption in the source.
Adjust the curved approach arrow to be longer and placed outside the arc between P and Q, matching the source direction cue.
